newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST - No Fed rate hike seen at Feb 4-5 FOMC.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - No Fed rate hike seen at Feb 4-5 FOMC.

text.p: U.S. economists expect the Federal Reserve to keep short-term interest rates on hold at its policy meeting next week despite recent news of a fourth-quarter 1996 growth spurt, a Reuters poll showed.

Twenty-five of 26 economists, surveyed after Friday's Gross Domestic Product report, forecast no move by the central bank's Federal Open Market Committee next Tuesday and Wednesday. Only one expert called for a move next week.
Although GDP growth accelerated faster than expected in the fourth quarter, inflation remains stable and growth should decelerate going forward, most survey respondents said.
GDP expanded at a 4.7 percent annual rate last quarter, according to the Commerce Department's initial estimate. Wall Street economists had expected a number between about 3.5 and 4.0 percent.
"I don't think this was enough to move them (central bankers)," said Tim O'Neill, chief economist at Harris Bank/Bank of Montreal.
Most inflation indicators, including the GDP price index, appear tame, Harris said. In particular, "the Employment Cost Index (ECI) was a calming piece of data last week," he said.
The ECI showed wages and salaries increased by 0.8 percent in the fourth quarter, below economists' forecast of 0.9 percent.

In addition, the chain-weighted price index, part of the GDP report, grew at an annualized rate of 1.8 percent last quarter, rather than the 2.2 percent rate projected by economists in a Reuters poll.
"You have a battle going on between the actual growth figure and the inflation readings," said Kevin Flanagan, vice president and an economist at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc.
The lack of clear inflation evidence should allow the Fed to wait for actual price jumps and avoid a preemptive move, several economists said.

"Most of the most recent news has been about the economy softening," said Robert Van Order, chief economist at the Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corp. "There is no reason to believe the Fed will have to try to slow the economy down."
Eight of the economists surveyed said the Fed could sit on its hands for the foreseeable future.
Another eight experts said the Fed may tighten credit in the first quarter, but most of those said that forecast depended on continued swift growth or a pickup in prices.
Nine more called for a rate hike in the second quarter or later, sometime after the next Employment Cost Index is released in April.

Wayne Ayers, chief economist at Bank of Boston Corp, said recent pronouncements from Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan sounded similar to the central bank chief's rumblings prior to the last tightening cycle, in early 1994.
"Back then, Greenspan was saying things like, 'this period of low wage growth and low price growth is probably transitional,'" Ayers said. "So I think he is really preparing for a move."
Although the preponderance of survey participants predicted a tightening as the Fed's next move, one economist said the Fed's next move would be a third quarter ease.
Full results of the survey follow.
Bank of Boston No May tighten 25/--
